title.narrative: Improving rice workers' conditions, human capital and resilience to reduce child labour risks in Punjab, Pakistan – Sustainable Scale-up Initiative

description.narrative: The project was executed in three project districts in Punjab, Pakistan: Sheikhpura, Nankana Sahib and Narowal. The activities conducted across all the project districts contributed towards creating the necessary knowledge and systems to ending child labour in the rice value chain. Some of the identified root causes of child labour risks in Punjab were economic poverty, low human capital (education/skills, healthcare), lack of alternatives for safe childcare during work hours, and seasonal/migratory nature of transplanting work.A combination of activities was conducted focusing on addressing some of these root causes, by improving working conditions during the planting season for workers and their children, awareness raising and training, as well as economic empowerment and improved livelihoods for rice farmers.Improving working conditions during the planting seasonShelters were provided during the transplanting seasons for approximately 22,800 farm workers and their children, providing them a safe space to rest, access water and shade and for the children to be cared for while their parents were working on the farms. Similarly, each planting season, free medical camps were organised at farm and village level in all three districts, benefiting a total of nearly 27,000 people. This helped rice farmers and their families access medical care more easily and at a reduced cost. Finally, Community Mother Centers (day care centers) were established and equipped with cognitive stimulating toys, books stationery, etc. Training was provided for community mothers (teachers) on cognitive-stimulating toys and civic education for children, nurturing their growth at the centers. This intervention built the capacity of mother day care centers to engage children and learn. A total of 255 children benefited from these facilities, where they enjoyed a variety of educational and recreational activities. The aim of the centers was to provide parents with an alternative to taking their children to the farm, and instead, leave them in the hands of trained educators and caregivers where the children would learn and develop their skills while their parents were working on the farms. All the Community Mother Centers have been handed over to the Literacy Departments of the Punjab Education Department, so that they can be sustained in time and benefit many more children. Awareness raising and training on safe and ethical labour conditionsTraining was provided on safe and ethical working conditions specifically for female farm workers. This initiative aimed to raise awareness among farm owners about the importance of creating a safe and supportive environment for their employees. As a result of the training, many farm owners took significant steps to improve conditions by ensuring the provision of clean drinking water and adequate shelter for their workers. Additionally, they recognise that fair compensation is essential for the well-being and dignity of their labourers. This shift not only enhances the quality of life for female farm workers but also promotes a more sustainable and productive agricultural sector.Apart from the above, 18 different sensitisation events were organised in schools to create awareness and increase knowledge of communities on the risks of child labour and the importance of human rights. These programs reached 20,800 youth and community members and actively engaged around 1,000 civil society members, group leaders, religious authorities, and government officials.Teachers play an important role in any community. The project chose to train teachers and engage them in the promotion of human rights, gender equality, fair labour conditions and reduction of child labour risks in their communities. A total of 15 teacher training programs were conducted, with 1302 teachers trained on human rights education across the three years (1000 teachers trained by the Foundation for Human Rights Initiative (FHRI) and 302 teachers trained by Care Pakistan). These teachers will play a crucial role in imparting human rights knowledge to future generations, contributing to a lasting impact on human rights awareness in the region.The teachers also played an important role in convincing about 300 children to come back to school instead of dropping out for work.Economic empowerment and improved livelihoods for rice farmers300 young people aged 13-17 years old have been enrolled in skills development programs to learn tailoring, machine embroidery, beautician, welding, plumbing, rice plant operator and cooking skills. Another group of youth have been enrolled in Technical Education & Vocational Training Authority (TEVTA) training centers. Some of these youth have been provided with start up kits to get their businesses going and others have obtained jobs in different sectors, supporting them to earn a decent income and contribute to their families livelihoods. Increased household income can help reduce child labour, but the relationship is complex. It is observed that families in poverty may rely on their children's income to meet basic needs. When household income rises, the reliance on child labour often decreases.In order to help families improve their livelihoods, the VSLA (Village Savings and Loans Approach) proved instrumental to increase the financial resilience of the poor rice planters’ families. Savings within their groups helped them to address their basic needs and invest more in children education. Increased enrollment in day care/learning facilities means more children are away from rice farms. This ultimately reduces the engagement of children in rice plantations. The linkage between community members and financial service providers significantly enhanced community resilience in several key ways; by establishing village savings and loan associations, families gained access to essential financial resources that previously may have been unavailable to them. This access enabled poor rice planters to save money collectively, allowing them to manage unexpected expenses and improve their overall financial stability. They were also connected with financial service providers so they know what kind of financial services and products are available in case they need any financial support to address their needs.Besides all the above, rice consortiums have been established in all three project districts. These consortiums are very helpful to ensure the sustainability of the above mentioned activities and also contributing in reduction of child labour. Over the reporting period, a series of activities were organised to raise awareness and promote key social, environmental, and economic initiatives. A total of 13 seminars were held, focusing on carbon credits, Sustainable Rice Platform (SRP) standards, human rights, child rights, and women's economic empowerment. These seminars were attended by approximately 2,700 participants, including rice farmers, mill workers, mill management, and community members.
